items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "monoculture".
items.answer: The growing of a single crop species over a large area
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the growing of a single crop species over a large area. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: A student claims: "Subsistence farming is always unsustainable." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Many subsistence systems (rotational farming, agroforestry, terraced rice) have been sustainable for centuries when population pressure is low.
items.markingKey: Many subsistence systems (rotational farming, agroforestry, terraced rice) have been sustainable for centuries when population pressure is low. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why monocultures are vulnerable to pests and diseases.
items.answer: Large areas of genetically similar plants provide abundant food for specialist pests, allow diseases to spread quickly and lack natural predators found in diverse systems (e.g. Panama disease in Cavendish bananas). (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Large areas of genetically similar plants provide abundant food for specialist pests, allow diseases to spread quickly and lack natural predators found in diverse systems (e.g. Panama disease in Cavendish bananas). (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Study the extract from the resource booklet.

Land use and calorie supply (Our World in Data, approximate): livestock (meat, dairy, and feed crops) use about 77% of agricultural land but supply about 18% of global calories and 37% of protein; crops for human consumption use 23% of land and supply 82% of calories.

Explain these differences using ecological principles.
items.answer: Livestock are at a higher trophic level, so energy is lost in respiration and heat (second law); more land is needed to grow feed or graze than to grow crops eaten directly.
items.markingKey: Livestock are at a higher trophic level, so energy is lost in respiration and heat (second law); more land is needed to grow feed or graze than to grow crops eaten directly. Award [1] per valid point or correct step, up to [2]; quoted data must include units; points must be drawn from the resource.

items.stem:
Case study extract - soy farming in Mato Grosso, Brazil: Brazil is the world's largest soybean producer (about 150 million t), much grown in the Cerrado and southern Amazon for animal feed exports.

Using the extract and your own knowledge, explain how this case illustrates commercial agriculture and its environmental impacts.
items.answer: Large-scale, mechanised monoculture for export drives habitat conversion and pesticide and fertiliser use.
items.markingKey: Large-scale, mechanised monoculture for export drives habitat conversion and pesticide and fertiliser use. Award [1] for each valid point linking the extract to commercial agriculture and its environmental impacts, up to [4]; at least one point must use detail from the extract.

items.stem: Give one strength and one limitation of the claim that subsistence farming is more sustainable than commercial farming.
items.answer: Sustainability depends on practices and population pressure rather than on whether a farm is subsistence or commercial.
items.markingKey: For: low inputs, local consumption, diverse crops. Against: low yields may drive expansion into forest. [4]: [1] for a valid argument for and [1] for its development; [1] for a valid argument against and [1] for its development; generic points with no environmental context are capped at [2].

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Farming to produce crops or livestock for sale at market, often large-scale and intensive"?
items.answer: commercial agriculture
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of commercial agriculture.

items.stem: Explain the difference between commercial agriculture and subsistence agriculture.
items.answer: Commercial farms produce for sale, often at large scale with high capital inputs and specialisation; subsistence farms produce food for the household, are usually small and use family labour and low inputs.
items.markingKey: Commercial farms produce for sale, often at large scale with high capital inputs and specialisation; subsistence farms produce food for the household, are usually small and use family labour and low inputs. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Compare a named commercial farming system with a named subsistence system in terms of inputs, outputs and environmental impact.
items.answer: e.g. soy in Mato Grosso (machinery, fertiliser, pesticides; high yields for export; deforestation and pesticide runoff) vs maize-bean farming in Malawi (family labour, little fertiliser; low yields for household; soil nutrient depletion).

items.answer: Intensification is part of the answer but must be sustainable, and reducing waste and improving access are just as important.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "Green Revolution".
items.answer: The increase in agricultural production from the 1950s-1970s using high-yielding crop varieties, synthetic fertilisers, irrigation and pesticides

items.stem: Compare biological pest control with chemical pest control.
items.answer: Biological control uses natural enemies (ladybirds, parasitic wasps) to reduce pests with few side effects; chemical control uses pesticides, which act quickly but can harm non-target species, persist and lead to resistance.

items.stem: Explain the difference between conventional (industrial) farming and organic farming.
items.answer: Organic farming avoids synthetic fertilisers and pesticides, relying on rotations, manure and biological control, usually with lower yields; conventional farming uses synthetic inputs to maximise yields but has greater pollution and fossil-energy costs per hectare.
items.markingKey: Organic farming avoids synthetic fertilisers and pesticides, relying on rotations, manure and biological control, usually with lower yields; conventional farming uses synthetic inputs to maximise yields but has greater pollution and fossil-energy costs per hectare. items.stem: Suggest three environmental impacts of large-scale palm-oil plantations.
items.answer: Deforestation and loss of orangutan habitat; peatland drainage and fires releasing CO₂; pesticide and fertiliser runoff; soil erosion; loss of biodiversity in monoculture.
items.markingKey: Deforestation and loss of orangutan habitat; peatland drainage and fires releasing CO₂; pesticide and fertiliser runoff; soil erosion; loss of biodiversity in monoculture.

items.answer: Transport usually accounts for under 10% of food emissions; land-use change and on-farm emissions (methane, N₂O) dominate, so what you eat matters more than where it comes from.

A land-use system combining trees with crops and/or livestock on the same land
Farming practices (no-till, cover crops, diverse rotations, managed grazing) aimed at rebuilding soil organic matter and biodiversity

items.stem: A farm of 1 ha produces 3 t ha⁻¹ of rice (3,600 kcal per kg). A person needs about 2,500 kcal per day. (a) Calculate how many people the crop could feed for a year if eaten directly. (b) If the crop is fed to livestock with an energy conversion efficiency of 5%, calculate how many people the resulting meat could feed. (c) Explain these results using ecological principles and discuss one reason why livestock farming may still be appropriate in some places.
items.answer: (a) 1 × 3 × 1,000 × 3,600 = 10,800,000 kcal ÷ (2,500 × 365) ≈ 12 people (b) 11.8 × 0.05 ≈ 0.6 people (c) each extra trophic level loses most energy as heat in respiration (second law), so eating producers supports more people; however, grazing animals can convert grass on land unsuitable for crops (steep, arid rangeland) into food and provide manure, income and nutrients.
items.markingKey: (a) M1 total energy ÷ annual need, A1 ≈ 12. (b) A1 ≈ 0.6 people. (c) R1 energy loss between trophic levels, R1 valid reason for livestock.

items.stem: Using the case study and your own knowledge, evaluate the view that the environmental costs of the Green Revolution outweigh its benefits.
items.answer: The benefits were enormous, but the environmental costs now threaten future production, so a "greener" second revolution is needed.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Green Revolution"?
options: Farming that meets current food needs while maintaining soil, water, biodiversity and livelihoods for future generations
The increase in agricultural production from the 1950s-1970s using high-yielding crop varieties, synthetic fertilisers, irrigation and pesticides
Chemicals such as fertilisers, pesticides and herbicides used in farming
Food fit for consumption that is discarded at retail or consumer level
items.answer: The increase in agricultural production from the 1950s-1970s using high-yielding crop varieties, synthetic fertilisers, irrigation and pesticides
items.markingKey: B. "Green Revolution" is the increase in agricultural production from the 1950s-1970s using high-yielding crop varieties, synthetic fertilisers, irrigation and pesticides.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "extensive agriculture"?
options: When all people at all times have physical and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food to meet their dietary needs for an active and healthy life
Farming with low inputs per unit area over large areas, giving lower yields per hectare
Food fit for consumption that is discarded at retail or consumer level
A crop whose DNA has been altered using genetic engineering, e.g. Bt cotton or Golden Rice
items.answer: Farming with low inputs per unit area over large areas, giving lower yields per hectare
items.markingKey: B. "extensive agriculture" is farming with low inputs per unit area over large areas, giving lower yields per hectare.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Growing different crops in succession on the same land to maintain fertility and reduce pests"?
items.answer: crop rotation

items.stem: Distinguish between undernutrition and malnutrition.
items.answer: Undernutrition is a deficiency of energy or nutrients; malnutrition includes both undernutrition and overnutrition (obesity) and micronutrient deficiencies.

items.stem: Explain how agriculture contributes to biodiversity loss.
items.answer: Conversion of forests, grasslands and wetlands to farmland; monocultures remove habitat diversity; pesticides kill non-target insects and pollinators; fertilisers cause eutrophication; hedgerow removal fragments habitats.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Conversion of forests, grasslands and wetlands to farmland; monocultures remove habitat diversity; pesticides kill non-target insects and pollinators; fertilisers cause eutrophication; hedgerow removal fragments habitats. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why commercial farms often have higher yields than subsistence farms.
items.answer: They use high-yielding varieties, synthetic fertiliser, irrigation, pesticides and machinery financed by capital and access to markets; subsistence farmers often lack money, credit, technology and secure land tenure.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They use high-yielding varieties, synthetic fertiliser, irrigation, pesticides and machinery financed by capital and access to markets; subsistence farmers often lack money, credit, technology and secure land tenure. items.stem: Distinguish between food waste and food loss.
items.answer: Food loss occurs before retail - during harvest, storage, processing and transport (common in low-income countries); food waste occurs at retail and consumer level when edible food is discarded (common in high-income countries).
items.markingKey: Food loss occurs before retail - during harvest, storage, processing and transport (common in low-income countries); food waste occurs at retail and consumer level when edible food is discarded (common in high-income countries). items.stem: Explain how dietary choices affect the environment.
items.answer: Animal products use more land, water and energy and emit more greenhouse gases per calorie because of trophic inefficiency and methane from ruminants; plant-based diets have much lower footprints.

items.stem: Explain the difference between chemical pest control and biological pest control.
items.answer: Biological control uses natural enemies (ladybirds, parasitic wasps) to reduce pests with few side effects; chemical control uses pesticides, which act quickly but can harm non-target species, persist and lead to resistance.
